description: Sabotages for windows-namespace-request-sys's allocation-failure paths (NR-3): an allocation that fails is an error the caller receives, never a panic or an abort. Run with tools/run-sabotage.ps1; see tools/README-sabotage.md for the format.
notCoveredHere: The allocation-failure paths (NR-3) have entries. The catalogue's other entries, the capture of handles and paths, and the security descriptor's own parsing are not covered. SecurityDescriptor::try_clone's failure is a declared blind spot (see its survives entry): AlignedBuf::try_clone allocates exactly the size of a buffer that already exists, so no test can make it fail. The failures of the two descriptor allocations, in capture and in conversion, are reached through their shared function, `allocate`, which the tests call with a length no machine has; the OS names the real length, so no descriptor can be made to ask for it. The volume and disk entries this manifest once covered, with the device-control helper, are in the win-volume-sys manifest.

sabotages.name: NR-3: a capacity the machine cannot supply is reported under another code
sabotages.why: A query whose buffer cannot be allocated reports ERROR_NOT_ENOUGH_MEMORY, the code a caller reads as 'ask for less'. Any other code would read as the call's own failure.

sabotages.name: NR-3: a descriptor allocation failure is reported as an invalid copy
sabotages.why: An allocation failure is its own failure, SecurityCaptureFailure::Allocate: an invalid copy would send a caller looking for a malformed descriptor.

sabotages.name: NR-3: a descriptor allocation failure carries the wrong code
sabotages.why: The error's raw code is ERROR_NOT_ENOUGH_MEMORY, which a caller who funnels everything through raw_os_error reads as 'out of memory'.

sabotages.name: NR-3: a copy of security attributes drops the descriptor
sabotages.why: A copy that kept the inheritance choice but not the descriptor would open files with different security than the original.

sabotages.name: NR-3: a failed security copy is reported as a failed duplication
sabotages.why: A request's try_clone reports a failed copy of its security attributes as HandleCaptureFailure::CopySecurity, not as DuplicateHandle, which would send a caller looking at a handle that was never the problem.

sabotages.name: NR-3: an open request's copy forgets its security attributes
sabotages.why: The copy must open with what the original would; the attributes went through Clone before, and nothing but this test would notice a copy that dropped them.

sabotages.name: NR-3: an open-by-identifier request's copy forgets its security attributes
sabotages.why: As for the path-named open: the copy must carry the attributes the original does.

sabotages.name: NR-3: a descriptor alignment that is not a power of two is refused by the build
sabotages.why: AlignedBuf refuses such an alignment and `allocate` reports every refusal as an allocation failure, so a bad constant would read as out of memory on every call. The constant is asserted where it is defined.

sabotages.name: NR-3: a batch alignment that is not a power of two is refused by the build
sabotages.why: As for the descriptor's: `perform` reports every refusal of the allocation as ERROR_NOT_ENOUGH_MEMORY, so a bad constant would be misreported as out of memory.

sabotages.name: NR-3: BLIND SPOT: a failed copy of a descriptor is reported as an invalid copy
sabotages.why: Declared blind spot, not a control. SecurityDescriptor::try_clone allocates exactly the size of a buffer that already exists, so no test can make it fail; the failure it would report is the shared `allocation()`, whose result the other entries pin.

sabotages.name: NR-4.1: a failed call's code is not the one the thread held
sabotages.why: The error an entry reports is the thread's last error, snapshotted in the statement after the call; any other value is a code the call did not produce.

sabotages.name: NR-4.1: control, the out-of-memory code written as its value
sabotages.why: A control: ERROR_NOT_ENOUGH_MEMORY is 8, so the file changes and no behaviour. A sweep that reports it caught is reporting everything caught and proves nothing.

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: a string is parsed at a revision Windows does not define
sabotages.why: SDDL_REVISION_1 is the one revision there is; any other is refused, so every string would be.

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: a descriptor is written at a revision Windows does not define
sabotages.why: As for parsing: the revision names the text format, and only one is defined.

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: a string with an interior NUL is passed to Windows
sabotages.why: Windows reads up to the NUL, so the string would be accepted as a different, shorter descriptor than it says.

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: the interior-NUL refusal carries a different code
sabotages.why: The refusal is made here, not by Windows, and its code is ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER, which a caller reads as it would Windows' own for a malformed string.

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: a string Windows refuses is reported as a failure to write one
sabotages.why: The two directions have their own failure, which a caller tells apart.

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: BLIND SPOT: a descriptor Windows refuses to write is reported as a refused string
sabotages.why: Declared blind spot, not a control. No descriptor and mask were found that Windows refuses to write, so the failure's kind cannot be reached from a test; the code it carries is read the same way as for parsing, which the other entries pin.

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: the mask asked for is not the mask passed
sabotages.why: The mask is which parts of the descriptor are written; passing another writes the wrong parts.

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: the text includes its terminator
sabotages.why: The text is the string and no more; a NUL on its end is a string no one wrote, and the reported length is not what tells it (it was measured to vary).

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: the text loses its last character
sabotages.why: The other half: a count one short cuts the string, which a length that does not count the terminator would do.

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: the group is named as the owner
sabotages.why: Each part has its own bit, and the names are the values Windows defines.
replace: pub const GROUP: Self = Self(GROUP_SECURITY_INFORMATION | OWNER_SECURITY_INFORMATION);

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: a selection contains only what overlaps it
sabotages.why: A selection contains another when every bit of it is set, and everything contains none.

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: BLIND SPOT: the memory Windows allocated is not freed
sabotages.why: Declared blind spot, not a control. A leak of this size is not observable from a test; the free is read from the code, which frees on every path through a guard.

sabotages.name: NR-3.1: control, the null check written as a comparison of the address
sabotages.why: A control: a pointer is null when its address is zero, so the file changes and no behaviour. A sweep that reports it caught is reporting everything caught and proves nothing.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: the reopen is made on no handle at all
sabotages.why: The original is the one input that says what is reopened; a null handle is refused by the call.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: the access asked for is not the access passed
sabotages.why: The access is the point of reopening; passing none gives a handle that cannot write.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: the share mode asked for is not the share mode passed
sabotages.why: Sharing nothing conflicts with the original, which is open and shares more.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: the flags asked for are not the flags passed
sabotages.why: A reopen that drops FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING returns a buffered handle, which accepts the unaligned transfer the test shows an unbuffered one refusing.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: the access getter answers the share mode
sabotages.why: Each getter reads back its own parameter; the values in the test are all different.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: the share-mode getter answers the access
sabotages.why: The other direction of the swap above.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: a new request starts with an access
sabotages.why: Nothing is defaulted: a request that says nothing carries nothing.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: a new request starts with a share mode
sabotages.why: As for the access: a default share mode would be a choice made for the caller.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: a new request starts with flags
sabotages.why: As for the access: a default flag would be a choice made for the caller.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: a copy forgets the access
sabotages.why: A copy is the same request.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: a copy forgets the share mode
sabotages.why: A copy is the same request.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: a copy forgets the flags
sabotages.why: A copy is the same request.

sabotages.name: NR-3.2: control, the zero share mode of a new request written as hexadecimal
sabotages.why: A control: 0x0 is 0, so the file changes and no behaviour. A sweep that reports it caught is reporting everything caught and proves nothing.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: an empty child is grafted
sabotages.why: Rule 1: an empty path names nothing, and the root with a backslash after it names the directory.
find:
let Some(first) = child.first() else {
        return false;
replace:
let Some(first) = child.first() else {
        return true;

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: a child that begins with a separator is grafted
sabotages.why: Rule 2: root-relative, UNC, verbatim and device paths are not relative to the directory.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: a child with a colon is grafted
sabotages.why: Rule 3: a drive-relative path and a stream name are resolved by Win32 from state this graft does not read.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: a separator is only a backslash
sabotages.why: Win32 reads a forward slash as a separator in an ordinary path, for the first unit and for every component.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: components are split at backslashes only
sabotages.why: A reserved name or a `..` after a forward slash is a component of its own.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: a parent component is refused whatever the directory
sabotages.why: Rule 4 is about a UNC directory only: under a drive-rooted one the `..` is collapsed by Win32 on the grafted path and means what it said.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: a UNC directory is one that begins with either separator
sabotages.why: Two separators begin a UNC path; one is root-relative, and a drive-rooted directory is neither.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: a parent component is any component that begins with two dots
sabotages.why: `..a` and `...` are names, not the parent.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: a separator is added whether or not the root ends in one
sabotages.why: A drive root and a root with a trailing backslash would be given a doubled one.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: a separator is added only when the root ends in one
sabotages.why: The other direction: the root and the child would be run together.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: a root with nothing in it is grafted onto
sabotages.why: The join would be `\child`, which is root-relative and names something else.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: the extension is not removed before the name is compared
sabotages.why: `CON.txt` is the device.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: the trailing spaces are cut one short
sabotages.why: The end of the name is one past its last character that is not a space; a cut one short loses a letter, and no name matches.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: the name is compared exactly, not without regard to case
sabotages.why: `con` is the device.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: a unit is compared by its low byte
sabotages.why: A unit that is not ASCII is not a letter, whatever its low byte is.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: the digits stop short of nine
sabotages.why: `COM9` and `LPT9` are devices.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: the digits start above zero
sabotages.why: `COM0` and `LPT0` are in Microsoft's list.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: the superscript digits are not digits
sabotages.why: Microsoft's list names `COM¹`, `COM²` and `COM³` too.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: any name that ends in a digit is a device
sabotages.why: Only `COM` and `LPT` take a digit; `CON1` and `AUX1` are names.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: NUL is not a reserved name
sabotages.why: D-19 lists it, and the rule errs toward not grafting.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: CONOUT$ is spelled without its dollar sign
sabotages.why: The name is `CONOUT$`, and `CONOUT` is a file name.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: LPT is not a name that takes a digit
sabotages.why: `LPT1` to `LPT9` are devices.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: the path handed to Win32 is the one given
sabotages.why: The graft is the whole point: a path that says nothing of the directory is resolved when the call is made.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: the terminated pointer is to the path as given
sabotages.why: The pointer is what the call reads, and it must be to the grafted path.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: the path as given is the one handed to Win32
sabotages.why: `given` is what the caller said, and a caller or test reads it to see what the graft did.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: a path that was grafted says it was not
sabotages.why: The flag is how a caller tells the two cases apart.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: the directory is read into a buffer of one character
sabotages.why: The size passed is the size of the buffer; a smaller one is reported as written and the rest is not.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: a size that fits is taken for one that does not
sabotages.why: The call answers the characters written when they fit, and the size needed when they do not.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: the buffer is not grown to the size the call asked for
sabotages.why: A directory longer than the first buffer would never fit, and the retry would give up.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: the failure of the directory call has no source
sabotages.why: The Win32 code is the cause and is reached through `source`.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: BLIND SPOT: the directory is read for a path that cannot be grafted
sabotages.why: Declared blind spot, not a control. A path that rules 1, 2, 3 and 5 refuse is returned as given either way, so a call that need not have been made is not observable from a test; the skip is read from the code.

sabotages.name: NR-3.3: control, the end of a name written with the operands of the sum swapped
sabotages.why: A control: addition commutes, so the file changes and no behaviour. A sweep that reports it caught is reporting everything caught and proves nothing.

sabotages.name: NR-3.4: a path with an interior NUL is accepted
sabotages.why: Win32 reads a path up to its first NUL, so the request would act on a shorter path than the one named.

sabotages.name: NR-3.4: OpenFile reports the path handed to Win32 as the path given
sabotages.why: The two accessors are how a caller sees what the graft did; swapped, they report nothing.

sabotages.name: NR-3.4: OpenFile reports the path given as the path handed to Win32
sabotages.why: The other direction of the swap above.

sabotages.name: NR-3.4: OpenFile hands CreateFileW the path as given and not the grafted one
sabotages.why: The graft is the point of capturing the directory: a relative path handed over as given is resolved when the call is made, against whatever the directory is by then. Only a test that changes the directory after building the request can tell, which is why it runs in a child process.

sabotages.name: NR-3.4: WatchDirectory reports the path handed to Win32 as the path given
sabotages.why: As for OpenFile.

sabotages.name: NR-3.4: WatchDirectory reports the path given as the path handed to Win32
sabotages.why: The other direction of the swap above.

sabotages.name: NR-3.4: WatchDirectory hands the call the path as given and not the grafted one
sabotages.why: As for OpenFile: observable only after the directory has changed.

sabotages.name: NR-3.5: ResolveFullPath accepts a path with an interior NUL
sabotages.why: GetFullPathNameW would resolve the part before the NUL and report success for a path that was not the one named.

sabotages.name: NR-3.5: control, the NUL test written as a search of the units
sabotages.why: A control: a string has an interior NUL when its units contain a zero, so the file changes and no behaviour. A sweep that reports it caught is reporting everything caught and proves nothing.
